items.title: Terry Pratchett's Study
items.content: My comment on Terry Pratchett's Study — Hacker News. Terry Pratchett once wrote about the concept of "horizontal wealth". Vertical wealth is where you spend money on rich people stuff - yachts and suchlike. Horizontal wealth is where you spend more money on the things you liked before you got rich: https://chibuikeani.blogspot.com/2017/02/the-price-of-happin... But horizontal wealth means not letting your increased income dictate your tastes. You like books and now you have money? Buy more books! Change those catenary bookshelves for good hardwood ones! In my case, build a library extension to your office. And, of course, you buy what will be useful for that most wonderful of pursuits, blind research, which is research without direction for the sheer joy of it. (Original source is his book A Slip of the Keyboard - this linked blog post quotes that bit.) Tags: hacker-news, terry-pratchett

items.title: parse_number() as a SQLite extension: C vs Rust
items.content: Research: parse_number() as a SQLite extension: C vs Rust I was out walking the dog when I got curious about how easy/difficult it would be to write a SQLite C extension that adds a parse_number() function for turning strings like -$1,234.56 or '12.5%' into numeric values that could be summed and sorted. I fired up regular Claude chat (Opus 5.5) and prompted: I'm thinking about a SQLite custom function 'parse_number(value)' that strips ',', '$', '£' and '%', handles a leading '-', and returns 'NULL' for anything it can’t parse Explore the difference between building this as a SQLite extension in C v.s. in Rust - I want to compare performance and code complexity and size of the resulting.so(or whatever) file This gave me a solid starting point - the Rust extension was 321 KB (using Rusqlite) and 298 KB (using sqlite-loadable-rs), while the C extension was 14 KB. But the Rust extension was faster! Turns out that's because the Rust equivalent of C's strtod is "twice as fast". So I prompted: Try writing your own C function for parsing text into a decimal number that catches up to or beats the Rust implementation And it did: Net cost per row over 2 million rows, lower is better: first C new C rusqlite sqlite-loadable Mixed data 67 ns 19 ns 46 ns 41 ns Integers only 25 ns 16 ns 36 ns 32 ns Decimals only 106 ns 18 ns 55 ns 47 ns Finally, I had it rewrite the prototype as a research report to match the others in simonw/research by prompting this: Clone simonw/research from GitHub and turn your above investigation into a research report as seen in that repository - you can give me a zip file to download that contains your new folder Here's the resulting report. items.content:
Most of the changes I make to my projects these days come in the form of PRs opened for me by Claude Code or Codex. The PR is my unit of work - I use them to bundle commits together, iterating on them until a feature is complete, document decisions and then merge the finished result. Today's coding agents are great at writing PR descriptions. They're too good at describing the work The problem is that they are too good. An agent-written PR description is accurate and comprehensive. It describes the problem, the detailed solution, and the steps taken to verify it. That's a lot of information to absorb. It's not necessarily slop, but it reads like slop! It's very easy to spot an AI-written PR, and as with other forms of AI writing my instant reaction is best summarized as "I'm not reading all of that". It doesn't matter how accurate or useful the information is, I'm instantly put off by the thought that it will take me longer to read than it took the driving author to write... even when that driving author is me! I want human editorial judgement. I want someone to have thought just long enough about the PR to give me a human-approved introduction that helps me understand, at a high level, what the PR is for and whether it deserves more of my attention. items.title: FasterRW: An Efficient Prior-Assisted Random Walk Solver for Thermal Analysis
items.author: Zixiao Wang, Tianshu Hou, Chenghan Wang, Zhen Zhuang, Leilei Jin, Tsung-Yi Ho, Farzan Farnia, Bei Yu
items.content: Thermal simulation is becoming increasingly critical in modern IC design and manufacturing. Feynman--Kac random walk methods can estimate localized temperatures without solving the global field, but in practical settings without Dirichlet boundaries they require very long paths to control the truncation residual. This paper presents FasterRW, a continuation-value framework for accelerating Feynman--Kac thermal random walks. We prove a stopping-time residual identity showing that the expected tail after truncation equals the current attenuation weight multiplied by the temperature at the stopping location. This identity enables a prior-corrected single-point estimator: a cheap, noisy prior replaces the unknown continuation value, making the truncation bias scale with prior error rather than absolute temperature and yielding an error-controlled threshold-selection rule. For multi-point queries, FasterRW further converts cross-query pass-through tails into pseudo-samples and refines the resulting observations in prior-error coordinates through kriging. Compared with prior state-of-the-art methods, FasterRW achieves up to $28\times$ acceleration while maintaining accuracy. Our code is open-sourced at https://github.com/ShiningSord/FastRW.

items.title: Embedding Consistent Recurrent Neural Networks in Finite Element Simulations for Path-Dependent Damage Prediction
items.author: Muhammed Adil Yatk{\i}n, Mihkel K\~orgesaar, Hasan Kurban
items.content: Capturing sheet-metal localisation physics with a trained surrogate inside a finite element (FEM) solver requires the surrogate to deliver consistent predictions irrespective of the solver's strain-increment count, which is difficult to control in non-linear explicit codes. We address this by re-implementing a trained recurrent neural network (RNN) damage criterion in Fortran and embed it as a live, increment-by-increment fracture criterion inside an Abaqus/Explicit user material subroutine (VUMAT), advancing the network state alongside the solver. Two architectures are compared: a SimpleRNN and the proposed Consistent RNN (ConsRNN), whose transition function is designed so that predictions converge as the strain path is refined rather than drifting with the increment count. Both are trained on bilinear strain paths and evaluated under varying temporal discretisations and nonlinear histories. SimpleRNN predictions drift as the increment count increases, which disqualifies it for embedding; ConsRNN converges under refinement, at a substantial fixed-resolution accuracy cost relative to SimpleRNN on multilinear paths. Deployed at structural scale, the embedded ConsRNN surrogate governs element deletion in a clamped steel plate and reaches the same peak force and peak displacement as an established two-parameter fracture criterion. This pre-peak agreement is expected by construction, since no element is deleted before the peak and the two runs therefore share an identical constitutive path; the responses diverge only on the post-peak softening branch. The results establish discretisation consistency as the decisive property for embedding recurrent surrogates in explicit FEM solvers, and report the first embedding of a customised, non-standard-transition recurrent cell at structural scale.

items.title: Rethinking Data Selection as Distribution Matching on Semantic Manifolds
items.author: Peng Sun, Yi Yang, Mingshuo Chen, Chunxiao Li, Yao Zhu, Huawen Shen, Tianfan Fu
items.content: Instruction tuning of large language models and large vision language models relies on massive training data, which incurs substantial computational and storage costs. Meanwhile, training data often contains redundancy, noise, and low quality samples. Existing data selection methods mostly rely on diversity, importance, or a combination of both, without explicitly constraining the distributional consistency between the selected subset and the full data in the embedding space. We propose QMAC, a quality aware multiband characteristic function matching method that formulates data selection as a joint optimization problem of distribution matching and quality filtering. QMAC matches the empirical characteristic functions of the selected subset and the full data across multiple frequency scales, capturing both global semantic coverage and local perturbations, while using task related quality scores to filter noisy and low quality samples. We systematically evaluate QMAC on 4 data types, 8 target models, and 44 benchmarks. Experimental results show that QMAC outperforms existing data selection baselines on standard image-text instruction data, substantially surpasses random selection on standard text instruction, image-text reasoning, and text reasoning data, and exceeds full data training in multiple model and budget combinations. The code will be made publicly available upon acceptance of the paper.

items.title: Generative Reconstruction of Full-Field Sensor States for Safety-Critical Digital Twins
items.author: Umme Mahbuba Nabila, Linyu Lin, Majdi I. Radaideh
items.content: Accurate reconstruction of incomplete sensor fields is critical for state awareness in safety-critical digital twins (DTs). Thermocouples in high-temperature and radiation environments may drift, fail, or become intermittently unavailable, causing partial observability. This study develops a sparse-sensor reconstruction framework for Oregon State University's High Temperature Test Facility (HTTF) and evaluates six methods under intra- and inter-experiment protocols: three conditional generative models (i.e., a diffusion model [DM], variational autoencoder [VAE], and generative adversarial network [GAN]), two deterministic recurrent neural-network models, and ridge regression. For intra-experiment reconstruction within the PG{-}29 depressurized conduction cooldown (DCC) test, the models combine graph-based spatial encoding with gated recurrent units. The graph neural network (GNN)--gated recurrent unit (GRU) VAE achieves the lowest error, with a mean absolute error (MAE) of $11.73,^\circ$C, a root mean square error (RMSE) of $20.54,^\circ$C, and an $R^2$ of 0.98. The deterministic GNN--GRU and plain GRU obtain RMSE values of $25.26,^\circ$C and $35.22,^\circ$C, respectively, demonstrating the benefit of spatial modeling. All three generative models reduce RMSE by more than half compared with ridge regression. The DM maintains an $R^2$ of 0.94 when known sensors decrease from 91 to 45. For inter-experiment reconstruction, models trained on PG{-}27 pressurized conduction cooldown (PCC) are evaluated on PG{-}29 using section-context conditioning. The section-context DM achieves the best transfer performance, with an RMSE of $42.84,^\circ$C and an $R^2$ of 0.91. These results demonstrate the value of spatiotemporal generative modeling for missing-sensor reconstruction in safety-critical DT applications.

items.title: Adaptive Depth Aggregation in Graph Transformers for Long-Range Graph Reasoning
items.author: Yifeng Lu, Zhen Wang
items.content: Graph Transformers improve long-range node-to-node communication through global or structure-aware interactions. However, improving cross-node communication does not determine how computations produced at different depths should be combined. Standard residual streams accumulate successive computations with fixed unit coefficients shared across nodes. This fixed aggregation is a residual-interface constraint: once intermediate contributions have been produced, the interface cannot explicitly reweight them by node. We hypothesize that this constraint can create a depth-wise aggregation mismatch when the relative utility of these intermediate contributions varies across nodes and structural contexts. To study this hypothesis, we formalize Graph Transformer residual computation as a causal node-wise history of graph-propagation and feed-forward network (FFN) contributions, making depth aggregation an explicit interface choice. We realize node-adaptive aggregation over this history with Attention Residuals (AttnRes) while preserving the backbone's graph-propagation and auxiliary-state machinery. Block AttnRes reduces the routing cost of long histories relative to Full AttnRes by pooling consecutive contributions. We instantiate the interface in GPS and GRIT and evaluate it on all five ECHO tasks. Both variants achieve lower mean absolute error (MAE) than their independently tuned backbones on every task, and at least one obtains the lowest mean among all compared methods in each task. Routing-only donor-swap interventions support the mismatch hypothesis, while additional ablations examine the key design choices. Together, these results support node-adaptive depth aggregation as a useful complement to cross-node communication in long-range graph reasoning.

items.title: Emergent Low-Dimensional Topological Dynamics Dictate Generalization and Escape Mechanics in Billion-Parameter Neural Networks
items.author: Dongqing Cao
items.content: The remarkable generalization of modern over-parameterized neural networks defies classical statistical learning bounds. Here we establish that optimization trajectories in billion-parameter models do not sample the ambient dimension $\mathbb{R}^N$ homogeneously; instead, they are dynamically constrained to a low-dimensional execution submanifold $\mathcal{M}_{\text{exec}}$ (with empirically observed effective dimension $d_{\text{eff}} \le 12$). By equipping the parameter space with a regularized Hessian metric $g_{ij} = \nabla_i \nabla_j L + \epsilon \delta_{ij}$ and analyzing stochastic Langevin diffusion on loss sublevel sets, we derive a rigorous Topological Generalization Bound grounded in projected subspace persistent homology. Furthermore, by linking Morse index transitions to Betti number annihilation ($\beta_1 \to 0$), we formulate an exact mathematical mechanism for exponential escape from strict saddles under anisotropic noise. We validate our framework across 80+ architectures (ResNets, Vision Transformers, and 7B LLMs). To bridge theoretical topology with computational feasibility, we resolve the curse of dimensionality by computing projected persistent homology proxies via randomized Lanczos iterations restricted strictly within active Hessian subspaces. Building upon this mathematical foundation, we introduce Topological-Adaptive Optimization (Top-SGD and Top-AdamW)---a family of wrapper algorithms that dynamically modulate learning rates using active curvature signatures. Extensive benchmarks demonstrate a 14.1\% reduction in total wall-clock training time on ImageNet with all computational and memory overheads fully accounted for. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/imslab-research/Topological-SGD.

items.title: Does Country Matter? Evaluating Geographic Sensitivity of Large Language Models in Zero-Shot Chronic Kidney Disease Screening
items.author: Sirajam Munira, Muhammad Ashad Kabir
items.content: Large language models (LLMs) show strong zero-shot reasoning capabilities, yet their sensitivity to prompt context raises questions about reliability in deployment. This study investigates whether geographic context embedded in prompts influences LLM-based chronic kidney disease (CKD) screening, independent of any change in patient features. Using a community-based CKD dataset from Bangladesh (284 participants with 112 CKD and 172 non-CKD), we systematically varied the country attribute across 25 global contexts while holding all clinical inputs constant, and evaluated two open-weight LLMs (Qwen3 8B and Mistral 7B). Experiments were conducted on a common-correct subset of 156 participants for whom both models produced correct baseline predictions. Results show that non-CKD predictions were highly stable across geographic contexts, with both models maintaining consistent non-CKD predictions in nearly all settings. In contrast, CKD-positive predictions were considerably more sensitive. For Qwen3, CKD prediction dropped from a baseline of 65 to as low as 50 across country contexts, while Mistral showed smaller but non-negligible variation. Country contexts did not group according to known epidemiological or healthcare similarities; instead, groupings appear to reflect how country tokens are internally represented within each model. These findings demonstrate that geographic tokens can systematically shift clinical screening outcomes despite identical patient inputs, with implications for the deployment of LLM-based decision support in diverse healthcare settings.

items.title: Interpretable Multifidelity Learning with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Spatiotemporal Nuclear Reactor Flow Modeling
items.author: Meredith Eaheart, Majdi I. Radaideh
items.content: High-fidelity computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations of nuclear reactor systems are computationally expensive, motivating machine learning methods that reduce cost while preserving accuracy. Multifidelity surrogate modeling addresses this by combining inexpensive low-fidelity data with limited high-fidelity data. This work investigates whether the high-fidelity data required to predict the spatiotemporal mass flow rate across all 193 fuel assemblies of a pressurized water reactor (PWR) core can be reduced, comparing black-box multifidelity feedforward neural networks (MFNNs) with interpretable multifidelity Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (MFKANs). Cross-fidelity correlation across the core is weak, making this a challenging multifidelity problem, and neither architecture predicts the transient particularly well in absolute terms. MFKAN nonetheless performs comparably to MFNN for one-time-step-forward prediction while also providing closed-form symbolic equations unavailable with MFNN. To address the scarcity of CFD transients, with only one available per fidelity level, TabDDPM-generated synthetic data was used to augment cross-fidelity forecasting. KAN and FNN achieve comparable self-evaluation accuracy (Pearson correlation of roughly 0.73--0.81), but both perform poorly at true cross-fidelity forecasting (correlations of 0.03--0.06). Assembly-level analysis shows that each assembly's forecast correlation tracks its real cross-fidelity correlation for both architectures ($r=0.840$--$0.896$ for KAN, $r=0.804$--$0.903$ for FNN), confirming that forecasting accuracy is fundamentally limited by how correlated the fidelity levels already are. Overall, KAN-based multifidelity modeling achieves accuracy consistently comparable to MFNN across all settings, while additionally providing symbolic equations that match or exceed the spline representation's accuracy.

items.title: What Are LLM Agents Actually Learning on Low-Budget Molecular Optimization Benchmarks?
items.author: Jiayu Qin, Zhengquan Luo, Changyou Chen, Zhiqiang Xu
items.content: Recent work reports large gains for LLM agents on low-budget molecular optimization. We measure the contributions of online optimization, retrievable task information, and permissive oracle landscapes. On PMO at 50 oracle calls, a GPT-4o mini agent's sum AUC falls from 14.44 to 4.85 after task names and curated reference compounds are hidden. An identity-blinded condition that states only the oracle form (e.g., similarity to a hidden reference) scores 5.39, while a deterministic retrieval-only baseline with no LLM reaches 12.16 (84% of the full agent). A full 23-task 2x2 ablation and a three-seed replication on eight tasks support this interpretation. On a protein-targeted benchmark with an AutoDock Vina composite oracle, a single-edit random walk is a strong lower bound; across three seeds it obtains composite 0.636 +/- 0.008 and docking improvement -1.11 +/- 0.04 kcal/mol. As a positive control, a retrieval-free population agent exceeds REINVENT at a matched 50-call AUC budget, with its strongest result at 100 calls. These results motivate two inexpensive sanity checks: retrieval-safe PMO prompts and a random-walk floor for docking-based optimization.

items.title: Evolutionary Adaptive Metric Learning: A Multi-Objective Framework for Learning Local Distance Functions in Nearest Neighbor Classification
items.author: Isaac Touza
items.content: Nearest neighbour classifiers inherit the geometry of their distance function. Fixed distances and globally learned metrics apply the same geometry throughout the input space, although relevant feature directions may vary across regions. We propose EAML (Evolutionary Adaptive Metric Learning), a framework that learns instance-dependent positive-definite metrics through a low-dimensional parameterization. Each local metric combines an input-dependent diagonal scaling, generated by softmax interpolation between anchor points, with a global low-rank correlation component. A real-coded elitist genetic algorithm optimizes the parameters using a scalar objective combining leave-one-out prediction error, robustness, metric smoothness, and regularization. We establish positive definiteness, metric equivalence, existence of an optimal solution, and Lipschitz continuity of the metric field. We further investigate prediction stability, generalization bounds, and evolutionary convergence under explicit assumptions. Experiments on synthetic data with region-dependent feature relevance show that EAML can recover local metric variations and outperform global metrics. Evaluation on thirteen public datasets using nested 5-fold cross-validation reveals a more nuanced picture: EAML improves performance on selected datasets but does not significantly outperform global metric baselines overall. Additional experiments show that global diagonal metrics can be preferable under nuisance features and test-time noise. These findings identify the conditions under which evolutionary local metric learning is beneficial and highlight its practical limitations.

items.title: How Small Can We Go? Calibrating Activation-Cache Compression for SAE Training
items.author: Abraham Yeung
items.content: To train a sparse autoencoder (SAE), you need a massive cache of model activations. We look into the effects that compression has on an SAE in two ways: we keep the original fp32-trained SAE and pass the compressed cache into the same SAE to see how many feature activations stay the same (the frozen-SAE test), and we retrain an SAE on the compressed cache and see how many of the original features still exist (the retraining test). We found that in the retraining test, there is no clear scale for retained features. On a GPT-2 cache, rounding everything to fp16 keeps 60.6% of features, but changing one value in a million by the smallest step fp32 allows (a change eight orders of magnitude smaller) keeps only 70.5%. Meanwhile, changing the random seed keeps 23.0%. For the frozen-SAE test, the frozen SAE's correlation with the original increases in order of how precise the codecs are, but plain $L_2$ distance gives nearly the same ordering. We also see the same frozen reading correspond to different percentages retained at different sites. This leaves the question of the right measurement. We build one by calibrating: retraining on identical bytes sets the ceiling, and a reseed sets the floor. We then measure the effect of each compressed codec against its own site's floor. With TopK SAEs on GPT-2 small and Pythia-1.4B at research-scale budgets, na\"ive per-token int4 loses more features than a reseed everywhere we tested, as do PCA and random projection on GPT-2. Standardizing each channel before quantizing brings int4 back above the floor in terms of retained features, at the same raw file size. At our smallest budget, a bf16 forward pass, which some pipelines use to save memory, loses slightly more features than rotated 8-bit storage. Calibrating a site costs four training runs and two evaluation passes.

items.title: Minimum-Sufficient Knowledge and Computation for Wind Energy Predictive Analysis
items.author: Purbak Sengupta, Aparna S. varde, Emil J{\o}rgensen Njor
items.content: Resource-constrained cyber-physical decision systems often apply fixed sensing, knowledge, and computational pipelines despite state-dependent information needs. We introduce Minimum-Sufficient Knowledge and Computation (MSKC), a resource-aware computing principle: select the least-costly route meeting decision-risk and deployment constraints, escalating only when cheaper routes are insufficient. As proof of concept, we isolate adaptive knowledge routing, the decision underlying Knowledge-Guided Machine Learning (KGML), which conventionally injects external knowledge unconditionally rather than only where needed. We instantiate this for wind ramp-event predictive analysis, an edge-oriented decision-support task, evaluating local, relational, and physics-informed routes with a state-aware gate on publicly available real data from two wind farms. We establish conditions for feasibility preservation, cost dominance, and strict expected savings over always-on routing. At a 35.9% relational-knowledge injection rate, adaptive routing is statistically indistinguishable from always-on injection on the reported metrics while reducing knowledge calls by 64%, supporting sustainable, Green-IT-aligned deployment. These results support MSKC's premise that uniformly maximal intelligence is unnecessary. This offers intelligent data analysis for big data streams: the analysis itself decides, per state, how much knowledge and computation the data warrant.

items.title: PINNeval: A Comprehensive Evaluation Standard for Physics-Informed Neural Networks
items.author: Kevin von Bargen, Hamid Ebrahimy, Tim R\"omer
items.content: The Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) literature has produced a rapidly expanding catalogue of methods. We divide a PINN training pipeline systematically into four components and observe that many existing benchmarks study these components in isolation. These components are domain-importance adaptation, loss balancing, neural network architecture, and optimization scheme. Moreover, the studies set the surrounding and not considered components of the pipeline to a minimal default that is no longer representative of current best practice approaches. Conclusions drawn under such conditions may not transfer to competitive pipelines. In this work, we propose a new evaluation protocol that (1) treats the four components as an integrated system; (2) crucially requires competitive implementations of the components not under investigation; (3) specifies the metrics and reporting format; and (4) is accompanied by structured documentation that ensures the traceability of evaluations across studies. Based on this comprehensive protocol, we release PINNpipe, an innovative JAX package containing 18 different methods from the current literature as well as nine efficiently implemented benchmark problems. Using PINNpipe, we illustrate our evaluation protocol in relation to established benchmark studies and report results that challenge common assumptions.

items.title: Not All Misalignment Is Alike: A Decomposed Benchmark for Emergent Misalignment
items.author: Afonso Domingues, Mubashara Akhtar, Bhada Yun, Xin Chen, Lukas Fluri, Anna Hedstr\"om
items.content: Emergent misalignment (EM), in which fine-tuning on a narrow task induces misaligned behaviour on unrelated prompts, has been demonstrated across a wide range of datasets, model families, and training setups. Yet, most studies continue to rely on the evaluation approach introduced in the original EM paper, producing rates that are sensitive to the small set of evaluation questions used, the choice of judge, and the thresholds applied. These evaluations can also conflate misalignment with capability loss and offer little insight into the specific ways misalignment manifests. Differences in datasets, models, and fine-tuning configurations further make findings difficult to compare across studies. We introduce EMERGE, a decomposed benchmark that tracks changes in eight distinct misaligned behaviours from base to fine-tuned models. It evaluates these behaviours on out-of-domain prompts against matched benign controls and tracks capability, coherence, and refusal to account for potential confounders. Applying EMERGE to 8 open-weight models and 13 fine-tuning datasets, we find that models with similar broad misalignment rates can exhibit very different behavioural profiles that a single score cannot capture. We hope EMERGE can help establish a shared and robust standard for measuring EM, making findings more comparable and helping move research from detecting the phenomenon towards understanding it.

items.title: Enhancing Academic Advisement with Case-Based Reasoning
items.author: Tanat Tonguthaisri
items.content: This research involved the study of an application of Case-Based Reasoning (CBR) in the field of academic advising. Academic advisement has been recognised as an important function of higher education. However, there is a widespread desire to improve the advisement services provided by many educational institutions (e.g., colleges and universities) around the world. In the last ten years, CBR expert systems have made important contributions in many domains by applying CBR methodology to a variety of areas of human problem solving. However, to date, expert advisement systems have not been successfully applied to academic advisement, which seems to be a very appropriate domain for this technology. Academic advising is an important and time consuming task, and different tools and techniques must be used to make it an effective and efficient process. This thesis describes the design, development, and validation of a prototype case-based academic advisement recommender system that supplements the conventional advising process, and could eventually evolve to replace human academic advisors when its full potential is realised.

items.title: NormGym: Evaluating Normative Competence through Social Interaction
items.author: Binze Li, Zihuan Zhang, Seokhyun Baek, Gillian K. Hadfield, Tianmin Shu
items.content: Normative competence, the ability to infer socially enforced expectations from interaction and adjust behavior accordingly, is essential for agents operating in unfamiliar human communities. Yet existing evaluations largely test whether agents can recognize or apply norms they may already know, rather than whether they can acquire previously unknown norms from social interaction. We introduce NormGym, an interactive benchmark for normative competence in which a newcomer must infer a hidden, arbitrary norm while pursuing its own task in a multi-agent community. Success requires distinguishing what is possible from what is permitted, inferring the norm from observed behavior and sanctions, and applying it in new situations. NormGym contains diverse norms and distinct environments, allowing systematic evaluation of current agents, including large language model (LLM) agents. We find that normative competence remains challenging: the strongest evaluated LLM achieves a joint task-and-compliance success rate of 55.3%. Our analysis reveals that models can sometimes revise their behavior following sanctions for their own actions, but struggle to use other agents' behavior and the sanctions they receive to infer the underlying norm. We further find that fine-tuning models may be insufficient to improve normative competence. These results suggest that current models lack a robust, transferable capability for acquiring normative knowledge through social interaction.

items.title: LLM-Based Feature Extraction for Multi-Criteria Inventory Classification
items.author: Humza Akhtar, Rami Pinto
items.content: E-commerce supply chains generate large volumes of customer feedback and operational data that remain underutilized in inventory management. Traditional inventory classification techniques such as ABC analysis rely primarily on annual dollar usage, while multi-criteria inventory classification (MCIC) methods extend this but still depend on structured quantitative data and do not utilize unstructured information available in modern supply chains. This paper proposes an LLM-based feature extraction approach that transforms unstructured sources such as customer reviews into quantitative features using vector embeddings and LLM-generated evaluation criteria. The enriched feature set is incorporated into an MCIC framework based on the Hadi-Vencheh model. Experimental results show measurable reclassification effects when customer sentiment signals are included, demonstrating that integrating unstructured data into MCIC can enhance inventory prioritization.

items.title: Benchmarking Machine Learning for Chaotic Three-Body Dynamics in Astrophysics
items.author: Sheng Wan, Pavan Vynatheya, Duo Xu, Li Kevin Wenliang, Ye Zhu
items.content: Machine learning (ML) and generative AI have recently made impressive progress in understanding physics. We explore a hierarchy of prediction problems stemming from chaotic three-body systems and benchmark existing ML approaches, including general-purpose prediction algorithms and those that build on top of foundational physics models. We first simulate the trajectories of triple systems near the critical boundary of stable/unstable initial conditions. We then design a hierarchy of learning tasks, focusing mainly on two broad problems: stability prediction and trajectory prediction. The former classifies whether a given triple system has diverged or not up to a specific horizon, while the latter predicts the exact trajectory, both given suitable input features. We benchmark a range of ML approaches, from simple regression methods to state-of-the-art foundational physics models, across these tasks, and compare them against astrophysical methods such as the Mardling-Aarseth stability criterion. Our experiments reveal a clear order of task difficulties in chaotic three-body dynamics: early dynamics enable strong stability prediction, while precise long-horizon trajectory forecasting remains difficult. Code and dataset are publicly available at https://github.com/Simonwan03/ThreeBodyMLBench.

items.title: Forcing a Letter Suppresses Refusal: Mechanistic Evidence from WMDP
items.author: Stepan Epifantsev, Anna Antipova, Oleg Chernikov, Leon Strelkov, Alexey Dontsov
items.content: Safety benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) commonly use multiple-choice question (MCQ) format. However, prior studies documented that MCQ format reduces refusal rates, which may significantly affect the safety behavior of the model. We provide a first mechanistic explanation of this effect on the Weapons of Mass Destruction Proxy (WMDP) dataset across two models - Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B. First, we use the tuned lens technique to show that when processing MCQ the model commits to an answer-letter token very quickly, which is in contrast to the gradual refusal build-up in open-ended formats. Additionally, we observe that activations on the MCQ format lie roughly 3x further from the refusal direction, compared with their open-ended counterparts. Moreover, ablating the attention heads that carry the MCQ format answer increases the refusal, which is a direct evidence that the MCQ answer-selection competes with refusal. These findings indicate that MCQ safety scores primarily measure knowledge capabilities and do not assess the safety-mechanisms.

items.title: Aspect-wise Pairwise Tournaments for Test-Time Selection
items.author: Hannah Guan, Yilun Du
items.content: Scaling test-time compute has proven highly effective at improving LLM reasoning. A popular method is best-of-n sampling, where a model generates many candidate solutions and one is selected. This motivates the question: how can we select the best candidate? When humans make choices, we find it more natural to compare two options than judge each in isolation. Additionally, when the options become complex, we like to judge the options one aspect at a time, such as comparing two job candidates on experience, communication, etc. In the test-time setting, candidate solutions should be judged in the same way. Here we introduce Aspect-wise Pairwise Tournaments (APT), which verifies by comparison and compares by aspect. Each matchup of a single elimination tournament is decided by a vote over multiple off-the-shelf aspect verifiers, each expressing a pairwise preference along its own aspect. Across five domains and three generator LLMs, APT improves over binary multi-aspect approval, self-consistency and reward model verification, with the largest gains on open-ended tasks. We find that both components matter; neither binary approval over the same aspects nor a generic pairwise judge at a matched budget matches APT. Because aspects are specified in natural language, APT also lets users steer selection toward properties they care about, better aligning with user preferences without needing to regenerate solutions. No component is trained, so APT transfers to new domains by simply rewriting prompts.

items.title: FinEvolveKG: Controlled and Attributable Prompt Evolution for Financial Knowledge Graph Construction
items.author: Abhinav Arun, Jayita Bhattacharyya, Fabrizio Dimino, Bhaskarjit Sarmah, Stefano Pasquali
items.content: Financial institutions construct knowledge graphs (KGs) from shared SEC 10-Ks to serve risk analysis, portfolio management, and investment research, whose analytical needs differ. Extraction must adapt without fragmenting shared grounding, typing, and temporal rules. Hand-authored persona prompts and fine-tuning add cost. Weight-free prompt optimization offers an alternative, but unconstrained evolution of a monolithic prompt can rewrite shared rules alongside persona guidance, obscuring changes and complicating review. We introduce FinEvolveKG, a KG-construction harness separating reusable general and persona-policy blocks and mechanically confining GEPA, a reflective prompt optimizer, to the designated block. During persona adaptation, the approved general block remains byte-stable and every optimizer edit is localized to a separately versioned persona policy. A dual objective balances generic temporal-KG quality with persona-relevant facts, motifs, and multi-hop connectivity. We evaluate five mutation scopes on ticker-disjoint 10-K splits, with three seeds for the persona-conditioned arms (v3-v5) across three personas. On the three-seed mean, the complete two-stage block-constrained workflow (v4) improves over the frozen prompt baseline (v1) by 19.4-30.9% and over the tested unconstrained full-prompt workflow (v5) by 2.2-6.4%, leading v5 on both objective components and winning all nine paired-seed comparisons with the lowest seed variance in every persona. Without further optimization, v4 also exceeds v5 across all evaluated out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts. An SME audit supports using the generated triplets as ground truth; a blinded two-SME audit favors v4 over v5 in 70.1% of contrast-enriched judgments. These results show that mechanically attributable evolution can coexist with strong empirical performance, without attributing the gains causally to the boundary.

items.title: Decision Context: Persistent Behavioral Learning for AI Agents
items.author: Nima Vahdat, Pashootan Vaezipoor
items.content: LLM agents do not learn from corrections across sessions. A user fixes the same mistake at the start of every conversation. Existing agent memory systems primarily handle facts, such as preferences, entities, and conversational history, rather than procedural knowledge. We present Forge Decision Context (forge_dc), a system that captures behavioral signals from human corrections and self-assessed tool-call failures, compiles them into imperative RULE directives, and injects them at the decision points where they apply. We evaluate forge_dc alongside four predecessor approaches on DC-Bench, a new benchmark of 71 scenarios across nine behavioral dimensions, built from real executed agent traces in a deterministic mocked-tool environment. forge_dc reaches 95% compliance, up from 55% with naive retrieval, while injecting approximately 10 times fewer tokens per query. Across the five-stage progression, the strongest systems represent behavioral memory as explicit directives and deliver it at the decision points where it applies. The results identify representation, activation, and placement as central design choices for persistent behavioral learning.

items.title: IWIBench: Evaluating Gradient-Free Model Driven Intra-weight Injection
items.author: Chris von Csefalvay, Pranav Doma, Achyuthan Unni Krishnan, Tam\'as F\"oldi
items.content: Intra-weight injection lets one model change another model's behaviour by editing its weights directly, without gradients. Such edits can range from altering lexical associations to enforcing output formats or updating factual knowledge. Despite growing interest in these approaches, there has been no systematic way to evaluate how well models perform them. We introduce IWIBench, which measures a large editor model's ability to modify the weights of a smaller target model (typically Gemma 3 4B IT) to achieve one of ten classical text-editing objectives while preserving its other capabilities. Editors are limited to four tools for reading and writing weights, with bounded tensor access and a fixed budget for generating and inspecting rollouts. A validator applies each proposed patch in a clean environment and compares the edited model against the unmodified target. Evaluating frontier closed- and open-weight models reveals sharply diverging capabilities, both across models and across tasks. A small number of models, most notably Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol, perform far ahead of the rest. The recency of this ability (little of it is evident in GPT-5.6 Sol, for instance), together with qualitative analysis, suggests it has been acquired through recent training. Tasks also vary widely: structured response resisted every attempt, and answer-length control yielded only one successful solution, whereas alias acquisition and recoding proved most amenable. Success in one task family correlated poorly with success in others, indicating an early and uneven capability frontier. We discuss strategies that editors repeatedly adopted and conclude with an outlook on intra-weight injection as an emerging but already potent approach to gradient-free behaviour modification.

items.title: Higher Order Component Attribution via Learned Surrogates in High Energy Physics
items.author: Lauri Laatu, Aritra Bal, Benedikt Maier, Markus Klute, Michael Spannowsky
items.content: Experimental High Energy Physics (HEP) has adopted the transformer architecture for identification of jets, particularly the state-of-the-art Particle Transformer (ParT) which injects explicit information about particle correlations into the attention mechanism. While able to achieve state-of-the-art results in accuracy, interpretability to its effectiveness has been limited. In this paper we propose component attribution methods using Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) that directly tie back to the physical descriptors of jets, to probe whether mechanisms such as Multi-Head Attention (MHA), or the ParT architecture, are able to learn these as discriminating features.

items.title: Pdb or Not to Be: Comparing Debugging Interfaces With Pass$_{X}$@$k$
items.author: Ryan Magnuson, Ellie Kitanidis, Ariel Lee
items.content: Interactive debuggers are indispensable to human software development, yet coding agents overwhelmingly rely on edit-execute-observe loops, using common bash tools, test scripts, and print statements to debug via repeated shell commands. Stepping through a debugger provides live access to runtime state, which may enable different problem-solving capabilities. However, prior work typically introduces the debugger as an additional tool or through a new subagent, making its individual contribution difficult to isolate from the associated scaffold changes. To address this, we compare a debugger-only agent against a bash-only agent on all 500 SWE-bench Verified instances, holding the rest of the scaffold fixed. We evaluate both architectures on two models, GPT-OSS-120B and Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B, with three independent runs per architecture $\times$ model configuration. Crucially, to distinguish interface specialization from expanded coverage under repeated sampling, we introduce pass$_X$@$k$, a cross-agent pass@$k$ that provides an unbiased estimator of the probability that at least one of $k$ agents is successful. Although the bash and debugger agents solve partially disjoint subsets of the benchmark in any single pair of runs, our pass$_X$@$2$ estimator reveals that this is largely due to run-to-run variance rather than tool complementarity. Across both models, we find that two bash rollouts outperform the combination of one bash and one debugger rollout. Our findings highlight the importance of accounting for stochastic variance in evaluating agent and tool diversity, and we hope that pass$_X$@$k$ will serve as a useful framework for the community.

items.title: AutoPYara: Next-Gen YARA Rule Generator for Malware Family Clustering
items.author: Mabon Ninan, Nhat Nguyen, Soumyajyoti Dutta, Sidharth Anil, Marcus Botacin
items.content: Millions of malware variants threaten users daily, such that clustering these samples is key for fast incident response. AutoYara is the current state-of-the-art for automatic YARA rule generation, but the task remains challenging on realistic datasets, where intra-family diversity and noisy clustering can degrade rule quality. We present AutoPYara, a solution armored with: (1) precise cluster centroid selection based on similarity hashing, and (2) an improved heuristic for estimating subclusters within a malware family using historical VirusTotal data. We implement AutoPYara as an open-source Python package (pip install autopyara) to support reproducibility and practical use. We show that AutoPYara, (1) increases rule coverage by 14 percentage points; (2) reduces variance by 7.1 percentage points, comparing the average variance AutoPYara exhibits to that of AutoYara; and (3) improves threat-hunting accuracy by 10%. AutoPYara produces robust and effective YARA rules than prior automatic approaches in practical settings.

items.title: AutoParallel: Composable, PyTorch-Native Automatic Parallelism for Production Training
items.author: Kaijian Wang, Sanket Purandare, Aditya Venkataraman, Will Constable, Ivan Kobzarev, Elias Ellison, Simon Fan, Edward Z. Yang, Davide Italiano, Patrick Labatut, Yuke Wang, Francisco Massa
items.content: Training large models requires multiple interacting forms of parallelism. As models and clusters scale, finding and maintaining efficient parallelization plans becomes essential for training performance. Diverse model architectures, workloads, and hardware topologies demand flexible strategies, yet production PyTorch systems typically rely on hand-written recipes that are costly to adapt and tend to reuse familiar patterns, which may be suboptimal for a given workload. We present AutoParallel, a PyTorch-native planner for distributed model training. AutoParallel searches parallelization choices jointly across the training computation, allowing established techniques to be combined and unconventional strategies to emerge. It expresses its decisions using native PyTorch abstractions and produces ordinary PyTorch programs, avoiding a separate execution runtime while composing directly with the PyTorch compilation and training stack. AutoParallel also composes automatic decisions with model-specific distributed code, allowing dynamic or specialized regions to remain under user control. Plans are inspectable and replayable artifacts. Across dense, hybrid, and mixture-of-experts models on meshes of up to four dimensions and 128 NVIDIA H100 GPUs, AutoParallel matches or exceeds expert-written TorchTitan recipes on most configurations, with throughput gains of up to 18.3%, and discovers plans that uniform expert recipes do not express.

items.title: CPU Micro-Architectural Characteristic Sensitivity Study on CPU-Side Agentic Task Latency
items.author: Jack Adiletta, Shixin Ji, Zhuoping Yang, Peipei Zhou
items.content: We perform a novel study of CPU micro-architectural characteristics on how they affect agentic AI CPU side latency. Small enterprises and individual users looking to reduce costs and seeking data privacy benefit from running agents locally, motivating an investigation into the optimal performance characteristics of an edge CPU to improve user experience. We investigate the relationship between CPU core frequency, CPU uncore frequency, active physical cores, and symmetric multi threading with agentic task latency in single and multi agent configurations. Across eight experiments on an Intel edge CPU, we find that P-core frequency produces the largest median latency improvement among the evaluated parameters. Increasing P-core frequency from 2.5 to 5.5 GHz yields a 1.154$\times$ speedup for a single agent and a 1.341$\times$ speedup for eight concurrent agents. We are the first to characterize hardware micro-architectural relationships on single and multi agent configurations with TerminalBench; we also provide an open source framework and dataset for repeatable CPU side latency agentic benchmarking.

items.title: ResServe: Accurate and Efficient FP4 LLM Inference with Residue Compensation
items.author: Shuo Rong, Ruibo Fan, Jiawen Wen, Xiaowen Chu
items.content: Block-scaled 4-bit floating-point (FP4) quantization reduces large language model inference costs but can degrade task quality. Higher-precision computation can mitigate this loss at the expense of some of the efficiency gains from FP4 inference. Narrow matrix computations common in decoding often leave spare hardware capacity for low-cost precision recovery. ResServe combines an FP4 activation base with an FP4-quantized residue representing information lost during quantization. It uses this spare capacity to compute the residue's contribution and combines results on-chip, avoiding extra result transfers. We apply this principle to linear layers and decode attention, while selective compensation limits added work when processing input prompts. On NVIDIA B200, compensated linear kernels using the NVFP4 format improve numerical precision while retaining latency close to uncompensated execution for the evaluated operations with few rows. In the evaluated NVFP4 inference configurations, ResServe adds at most 3.4% request-latency overhead over W4A4 and reduces request latency by 22.4-53.3% relative to W4A8. Across five models, code-generation accuracy improves over same-format uncompensated inference, with mean relative gains of 15.04% for NVFP4 and 53.57% for MXFP4.

items.title: The GPU Needs an Operating System
items.author: Reza Nourai, Behnam Bastani
items.content: AI chips sit mostly idle while serving models, because replies must be fast and each step waits on memory. On two large open models, the math units were busy only about 6-11% of the time. We argue the GPU needs an operating system that keeps urgent work on schedule and fills idle capacity with other useful work. A feature that ships today recovers a quarter of a GPU with work designed to share, and a tenth with real jobs, at 5% slower decode. Our research system does better: one resident kernel runs a whole model faster than vLLM's best for a single request, and shares the GPU at under 2% slowdown. Scaling beyond one hand-built model needs compilers and a few new chip features, which we specify.

items.title: I Don't Care How You Hide It, I Care What You Do: Runtime Detection of Malicious ML Models
items.author: Hala Ali, Andrew Case
items.content: Pre-trained machine learning (ML) models shared through public platforms can be weaponized to execute malicious payloads during loading or inference. Existing scanners prove inadequate for detecting malicious models as they rely on static analysis and function denylists, support limited serialization formats, and miss attacks that replace denylisted functions with equivalent alternatives, exploit unsupported loading paths, or abuse legitimate framework APIs. To address this problem, we present ModelShield, the first runtime behavioral detection system for malicious ML models that attributes observed system-level behavior to specific model operations. It combines application-level instrumentation of ML framework APIs with eBPF-based syscall tracing, tracking model behavior across spawned threads and processes to separate model-triggered activity from environment noise. Attributed syscall sequences are classified using 195 detection patterns mapped to MITRE ATT&CK techniques. We implemented ModelShield to support 17 ML frameworks and 36 formats. On an independent dataset, it is the only evaluated tool to achieve zero false positives, with false negatives limited to payloads that produce no malicious runtime behavior. It detected all 29 published evasion variants spanning function substitution, loading-path obfuscation, and TensorFlow API abuse, where no existing scanner achieved complete coverage. Across 145,000 models scanned from public platforms, it captured 41 malicious models on Hugging Face, including a reverse-shell payload and a payload that performed host reconnaissance and outbound exfiltration. Among these, ModelScan, PickleScan, Fickling, and ModelAudit detected only 29%, 56%, 80%, and 93%, respectively. Despite runtime overhead, ModelShield has a median analysis time of 12.3 seconds, with 90% of scans completing within 35.5 seconds, making it practical for hub-scale screening.

items.title: Conflux: Preventing Privilege Escalation with Principal Contexts and System-Level Evaluation
items.author: Raya Buckley, Christian Schroeder de Witt
items.content: LLM agents combine information from multiple principals while acting externally. We formalise privilege escalation (PE) as the system-level security objective: an action may proceed only if every principal that influenced it would allow it. Model-level defences remain probabilistic, so enforcement must sit outside model judgement. We present Conflux, a principal-context defence. Its kernel, ITES, derives authority from provenance and the organisation's existing access-control system and intersects the permissions of every influencing principal. We prove a conditional authority-confinement theorem: under complete mediation, no-laundering provenance, a known non-empty decision context, fresh permission checks, and action binding, the kernel admits no action that escalates privilege with respect to any recorded influencing principal. The theorem covers the represented value-influence fragment; control influence from tool, branch, recipient, or plan-step selection remains a refinement obligation. Conflux extends the kernel with independent policy ports, argument-aware authorisation, disclosure, consent, delegation, restriction, and exposure planning. We describe two system- level evaluators. SLED is a black-box evaluator: it exhaustively explores a declared finite model of a defence up to a bound. SLED-V is a white-box evaluator: it checks a serialisable intermediate representation against security and provenance properties. The evidence is bounded and partial. The appendix reports retained AgentDojo, SLED, and SLED-V results, including the limits of those runs. No result in this paper is an unbounded deployment guarantee.

items.title: ReKV: Overlapping Quantized KV Transfer and Suffix Recomputation
items.author: Guangjian Dong
items.content: Prefill--decode disaggregation moves a prompt's key--value (KV) cache between workers before the first token can be generated. Reducing this handoff to either cache compression or recomputation misses a useful choice: which layers to transmit, at what precision, and which layers to execute again on the decode worker. ReKV transfers a quantized prefix KV cache and one BF16 boundary state, then reconstructs a contiguous suffix while the prefix is in flight. In a model-shaped synthetic benchmark on cross-node H100s, the Q8 configuration meeting separately evaluated quality criteria reduces 8K handoff latency by $2.36\times$, $2.84\times$, and $3.65\times$ over BF16 transfer for Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-3B, and Qwen3-8B. It is also faster than the best measured transfer-only or recompute-only action at those points. A separate real-weight BF16 recomputation experiment reduces prefill-to-token-return time by $1.16$--$1.63\times$. The preferred action changes with prompt length and link bandwidth.

items.title: Gain-Dependent Entropy Characterization of a Zener Avalanche Noise TRNG via Dual NIST Standards: Toward Low-Cost Hardware Entropy for ICS Deployments
items.author: Rishabh Das
items.content: True random number generators based on Zener avalanche noise offer a low-cost entropy source for industrial control system and IoT edge devices, yet the relationship between amplifier gain, coupling capacitance, and entropy quality remains uncharacterized under current NIST standards. This paper presents a comprehensive entropy assessment of an op-amp-based Zener avalanche noise generator across five gain configurations and two coupling capacitor values, evaluated against the NIST SP 800-22 statistical test suite and the SP~800-90B entropy source assessment using 1.44 billion raw bits per configuration. We identify a three-phase autocorrelation structure, attributed to comparator saturation-recovery dynamics, consistent across all gain settings. A direct-current substitution experiment, replacing the Zener diode with a stable voltage source at the same bias point, reduces switching activity by approximately 97%, confirming that Zener avalanche noise, rather than amplifier self-excitation, is the necessary entropy source. The coupling capacitor is further shown to govern comparator overdrive and entropy quality independent of this source mechanism, with the smaller capacitance improving entropy, throughput, and bias. The combined results identify an optimal gain configuration achieving a perfect statistical test score, NIST-compliant min-entropy, and peak entropy throughput at a bill-of-materials cost under five dollars, offering practical design guidance for low-cost entropy sources in industrial and embedded deployments.

items.title: Jev as an LLM Safety Guardrail: An Empirical Study of Input Filtering, Selective Output Review, and Over-Refusal
items.author: Olivia Cognetti, Bhaskar Krishnamachari
items.content: External safety filters can prevent unsafe requests from reaching a large language model (LLM), but may also reject legitimate queries. We present an end-to-end empirical evaluation of Jev, a probabilistic decision model, as a safety guardrail for a Qwen2.5-1.5B-based pipeline. Three configurations are compared on 970 benchmark prompts: an unfiltered LLM, Jev input filtering, and tiered Jev input filtering with selective output review. Across 720 prompts labeled harmful (520 AdvBench and 200 XSTest-unsafe), the fraction recorded as answered decreases from 527/720 (73.2%) without filtering to 17/720 (2.4%) with input filtering. On 250 XSTest-safe prompts, however, non-answer/refusal increases from 3/250 (1.2%) to 27/250 (10.8%). Tiered filtering yields 40/720 (5.6%) harmful-prompt answers and 10/250 (4.0%) benign-prompt refusals, with 79/970 (8.1%) of prompts requiring output review. Joint optimization of the tiered thresholds improves macro-F1 from 0.9351 to 0.9512, while reducing harmful-prompt answers and output-review frequency at the same benign-refusal rate. Matched-budget comparisons reveal modest additional gains over a retuned single gate on the evaluation data, although these gains are not consistently observed on a held-out split.

items.title: Adaptive Scheduling Pipeline for Multi-Instance Asynchronous Reinforcement Learning
items.author: Salah Chikhi, Luis Zuin, Entong Li, Zeng Li
items.content: We present the Adaptive Scheduling Pipeline (ASP), an offline rollout scheduler for multi-instance asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) of large language models (LLMs). ASP jointly reduces three sources of rollout underutilization - padding bubbles from intra-minibatch length heterogeneity, skewness bubbles from long-tail outputs, and sorting bubbles from fluctuations in training-queue occupancy induced by length-sorted dispatch - through a single offline preprocessing pass. This enables efficient multi-instance rollout that overcomes the early scaling plateau of single-instance inference while smoothing the arrival of generated samples at the trainer. We integrate the scheduler into an asynchronous architecture that decouples rollout from training while keeping policy lag observable and bounded. Complete ASP improves end-to-end throughput by up to 3.22 times and reduces iteration time by up to 76.8% relative to MindSpeed-RL, while reducing iteration time by up to 62.5% relative to verl. Within ASP, scheduling reduces mean iteration time by 10.9%. ASP also scales more robustly with additional generation resources than these baselines and shows no visible convergence degradation in the measured bounded-lag regime. ASP has since been used in an internal telecom-domain RL post-training workflow, reducing the reported training period from more than three months to about two months and producing a domain-enhanced model for knowledge answering and tool calling.

items.title: Who's Asking? Audience-Conditioned Privatization
items.author: Daniil Filienko, Anusha Bagalkotkar, Xan Vongsathorn, Sikha Pentyala
items.content: The abundance of user-generated conversational data makes the question of how to responsibly derive insights from confidential data without putting the individuals in it at risk ever more important. However, the majority of existing differentially private (DP) synthetic text generation (SDG) and anonymization approaches ignore the context of the data's downstream usage, which results in loss of important information. DP-SDG provides the same guarantee regardless of the recipient, and anonymization relies on predefined attribute categories. They both ignore the observation that an attribute that is harmless to one audience can be sensitive to another, and each audience typically needs only some attributes preserved. We propose Ext-Classify-Priv, a framework that (1) extracts the information types present in a corpus, (2) classifies which of them are private for a given audience following contextual integrity, and (3) protects only those attributes, using either anonymization or SDG with Feature-DP approaches. On Reddit data with 3 audiences, our audience-specific releases are more faithful than a single audience-agnostic release for every audience. On bioRxiv data, our SDG method improves MAUVE from 0.097 to 0.420 at epsilon=1 and on the proprietary real estate data, our anonymization method improves MAUVE from 0.698 to 0.959 over the best baselines.

items.title: Inside the Trap: A Renewal Law for Prefix-Cache Collapse in LLM Agent Serving
items.author: Akshat Valse, Ali Jannesari
items.content: Prefix caching lets an LLM agent's follow-up turns reuse cached KV, but a burst can tip an engine into a trap in which every turn misses and the backlog does not drain, at a load it served before. In registered paired tests on two engines, two GPUs and two models (passed at 9 of 10 rates), a 200-session burst left the engine at zero hits to the end in all 30 runs, while every matched no-burst run stayed good and a session cap prevented the trap in all 30 capped runs. We analyse an idealization of the trapped state exactly: for a fluid FIFO server on which every turn misses, we prove that along FIFO orbits its cycles obey a linear renewal recursion. As is classical, the trap drains if and only if arrivals are below the all-miss capacity; above it, a Perron root fixes the dynamics: every trapped state converges to a known self-similar regime in which the gap between turns grows linearly and the turns served are young and short. For our workload the backlog grows at 0.6 to 0.8 of the excess load and sessions complete faster than the all-miss capacity, a youth premium with turn-count and cost-growth factors, so in the model a trap's measured throughput overstates the recovery threshold. Retrospectively, with nothing fitted to trap data, the theory matches 57 stuck runs: the mean served prompt within 3% in 50 runs, completions above the all-miss capacity in every run, and the pooled gap growth. Blind in outcome, 4 runs trapped by a tool slowdown met 4 of 5 pre-set scores, cut traps persisted, and with a 20-step budget, trapped runs completed below the all-miss capacity, as predicted. Of two exits, refusing arrivals sheds sessions; a session cap restores reuse: in registered tests it rescued 9 of 9 established traps at the same load without shedding, and the engine stayed good after release. We do not prove that the engine converges to the model.

items.title: LLM-Augmented Flow for Project Conformation and Task Complexity Evaluation Based on the TLM Framework
items.author: Maksim Sysoev, Alexander Semenov, Ilia Cheshev, Alexey Gevorkyan, Danil Somov
items.content: The software development process, from inception to a working product or solution, can be divided into two major phases: discovery (Discovery) and delivery (Delivery). The Discovery is further subdivided into High-Level Discovery (HLD) and Low-Level Discovery (LLD). During HLD, management identifies the business solution or product to be integrated into the company's infrastructure. LLD, in turn, produces requirement documentation artifacts, including the Product Requirements Document (PRD), Business Requirements Document (BRD), and Functional Specifications Document (FSD). Story Points (SP) are a widely used modern approach to measuring the effort required to accomplish predetermined tasks, and the artifacts listed above help derive SP more precisely. With the rapid growth of LLM technologies, one of the main questions that arises is whether the whole Discovery phase, or most of it, can be completed with the help of LLM tools. In this paper, we test a framework that structures requirement documentation generation and task complexity scoring, based on the model introduced by (Tran, L\'evesque, and Meunier 2004) and executed with the help of agentic tools. The approach is applied to a real-world commercial project in the fintech domain as a feasibility study rather than a validation: development effort was not recorded for the tasks examined, and the resulting complexity scores are therefore reported as the output of the instrument rather than as validated estimates of effort.

items.title: DRAFT-Bench: Evaluating Frontier Agents Across the Professional Design Lifecycle
items.author: Rong Pan, Jianqiang Wang
items.content: Can frontier general-purpose agents understand client intent, explore creative directions, execute revisions, and prepare production deliverables? We introduce DRAFT-Bench (Design Reliability Across Feedback and Tasks), a lifecycle-oriented evaluation of requirement elicitation, creative exploration, constrained editing, iterative revision, and production handoff. Its Requirement-to-Artifact framework links evolving requirements, protected properties, artifact versions, and delivery obligations. We compare native Codex/Astra and Claude Code across 35 design briefs under 43 conditions, alongside a separate 40-scenario RFQ track. Astra completes 43/43 design conditions and Claude 35/43. All scored core runs receive full structural credit, yet on the 28 core conditions scored for both systems, semantic checks flag violations in 11 for Astra and 5 for Claude; these are model judgments, not expert-confirmed failure rates. RFQ coverage is high, but success ordering changes across cohorts. SKU expansion, revision dependencies, and White ink files expose ambiguity among unmet obligations, missing inputs, and evaluator interpretations. These findings separate execution, requirement compliance, and professional acceptance. Unpaired tracks and different tools preclude claims of RFQ-to-delivery success, factory acceptance, or a pure model ranking.

items.title: More with Less: Efficient Parallel Scientific Code Translation via an Agent-Skill Workflow
items.author: Jianuo Shen, Pengyi Xu, Bo Zhang
items.content: Translating parallel scientific codes between HPC programming frameworks is a critical but labor-intensive task. Existing LLM-based approaches rely on fixed sequential pipelines with undifferentiated repair strategies and correctness criteria that do not match scientific computing practice. We present an agent-skill framework that separates translation, compilation diagnosis, and execution validation into three autonomous agents coordinated by a verdict-driven orchestrator, routing each failure to a targeted repair skill rather than retrying blindly. An automated output check drives the self-correction loop, complemented by an offline LLM-based verification that exposes false positives escaping compiler and runtime checks. We evaluate the framework on 30 HeCBench kernels translated bidirectionally among CUDA, OpenMP, and SYCL with three open-source LLMs. Our framework attains the higher verified correctness rate in all 18 model and direction combinations over a state-of-the-art baseline while consuming up to 52.4% fewer tokens, remaining consistent across models and directions without architectural modification.

items.title: NotaryMark: Multi-Bit Watermarking for Black-Box DatasetUsage Auditing in Text-to-Image Diffusion Models
items.author: Xinyi Yu, Linkang Du, Zhou Su, Min Chen, Yuntao Wang, Zhikun Zhang
items.content: As generative artificial intelligence (AI) models increasingly require data, more publicly available yet licensed data is being harvested and used without authorization. Although several previous studies have proposed watermarking methods for dataset copyright auditing, their applicability to the text-to-image (T2I) setting remains notably limited. The core drawback is that watermarks embedded by existing techniques are often treated as noise and are gradually filtered out and attenuated during the latent noising-denoising process of diffusion model training. We propose NotaryMark, to our knowledge the first multi-bit watermarking method specifically designed for black-box auditing of T2I training dataset use. The core idea of NotaryMark is to align the watermark with the latent denoising of diffusion models, thereby overcoming the signal decay that plagues existing multi-bit methods during sampling. We evaluate NotaryMark across three datasets and three diffusion models spanning watermark capacities from 8 to 1024 bits. With a watermark capacity below 32 bits, it achieves a high average bit accuracy of 0.85-0.90. With a watermark capacity exceeding 32 bits, it maintains bit accuracy between 0.67 and 0.80, consistently outperforming existing multi-bit watermark methods whose bit accuracy is around 0.42-0.60. Furthermore, we design a voting-based aggregation scheme to boost the bit accuracy with a modest budget of 30 queries. Building on this, we incorporate error-correcting codes to enable reliable decoding and tracing of the embedded identifier information. Robustness evaluation against fifteen evasion attacks spanning seven categories shows that NotaryMark remains robust under most evaluated settings, while stronger attacks generally suppress watermark evidence only at the cost of substantial utility degradation, demonstrating its practical reliability against malicious tampering.

items.title: Capital Efficiency, Isolation, Risk, and Ruin in Generative AI Inference Serving Infrastructure
items.author: Ren\'ee St. Amant, Anjaly Parayil, Ankur Mallick, Victor R\"uhle
items.content: Generative AI serving is an extremely capital-intensive endeavor that demands rapid, step-change improvements in capital efficiency to prevent industry wide increases in the cost of capital from limiting growth plans. Keeping pace with the economic necessities will increasingly require infrastructure providers to confront operationally-inconvenient realities of production serving, including the extreme heterogeneity of generative AI request costs. We have explored workload isolation as a foundational, fleet-level lever for increasing capital efficiency. Isolation is the practice of intelligently grouping "like" requests before execution. Rather than exposing every replica to the full heterogeneous workload distribution, isolation deliberately reshapes the workload presented to the hardware by assigning requests with different cost characteristics to different portions of the fleet. Workload isolation on its own does not make expensive requests cheaper; it prevents a costly portion of the workload from unnecessarily determining the operating point and capital efficiency of the entire fleet. It additionally lays the foundational groundwork that can serve as a launching point for compounding gains via narrow-band optimizations (tailoring) and custom silicon designs while also informing up on pricing policy. This paper uses representative production data and experience to convey the motivation behind isolation as a fleet-level lever for increased capital efficiency.

items.title: ISER-MoE: Dynamic In-Switch Replication of Hot Experts for Load Balancing in Expert-Parallel
items.author: Jintao Peng, Ethan Zhang, Kefeng Duan, Bangyu Sheng, Min Li, Itamar Rosenfeld Rauch, Jack Yang, June Yang
items.content: Expert-parallel mixture-of-experts (MoE) layers run at the pace of the most loaded GPU, and a few hot experts carry most of the excess load. Replicating them at every MoE layer balances the load only if their weights arrive within the layer, and broadcasting from the owner is the bottleneck: point-to-point copies overload it, and baseline broadcasts pay latency or bandwidth overheads. We present ISER-MoE (In-Switch Expert Replication for MoE), built in TensorRT-LLM, which multicasts hot experts through the NVLink switch to fixed GPU groups, so each byte leaves its owner once. A GPU scheduler assigns hot experts to groups per layer, and a multi-port broadcast spreads the injection over the group's ports, both overlapped with the shared expert. In trace replay, the scheduler removed 98-99% of the excess load; in prefill serving of DeepSeek-V4-Pro, throughput rose 17.4% on a math benchmark and 7.2% on agentic prompts.

items.title: Beyond a Single Commit: Anchor-Guided Reconstruction of Multi-Commit Patches
items.author: Jialiang Dong, Willy Susilo, Xu Gai, Liuhuo Wan, Chao Zhang, Elisa Bertino, Siqi Ma
items.content: Vulnerability patch identification plays a critical role in software security by linking reported vulnerabilities and the corresponding fixes, enabling reliable vulnerability analysis, mitigation, and automated security tool development. As software systems evolve in complexity, vulnerability remediation has increasingly shifted from single-commit fixes to multi-commit fixing processes. Although many studies have been proposed to identify fixing commits associated with target vulnerabilities automatically, they often suffer from inaccurate semantic analysis or excessive workload for language models. These limitations reduce both the effectiveness and comprehensiveness of fixing commit identification. To improve patch identification, we propose an effective and comprehensive patch identification framework, HARPOON, which not only enhances the accuracy of identifying individual fixing commits, but also investigates dependencies among commits to achieve comprehensive commit recognition for target vulnerabilities. Experimental results show that HARPOON significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art approaches. HARPOON successfully identified 895 vulnerability patches that were not previously maintained in public vulnerability databases. Among them, 663 are previously unrecorded fixes associated with 323 CRITICAL- or HIGH-severity vulnerabilities.

items.title: MongoBench: Do LLMs Know What a MongoDB Query Will Do?
items.author: Qibai Chen, Haoting Qiu, Yezhou Cheng, Mengxiao Qian
items.content: LLM agents increasingly operate databases on their own: they generate queries and run them against live data. Two checks are commonly used to judge such an agent - whether it produces a valid query, and whether it reaches the right final answer - but neither tells us whether the agent knows what its query will actually do before it runs. We argue that this consequence prediction ability must be evaluated in its own right, and we build MongoBench to measure it: given a collection of documents and a MongoDB find() filter, a model must return the exact set of matching _ids, with ground truth from a real mongod server. The 300 items each compose three or four documented matching pitfalls and are proposed symmetrically by three vendors' models, so results stratify by item source. Evaluating four models - frontier systems from three vendors and one open-weight reasoner - accuracy ranges from 70.1% to 92.1%, a 22-point spread. Each proposer mispredicts 10-31% of the items it wrote itself, so producing a query does not imply predicting its effect. A failure-mode analysis shows errors are better predicted by which semantic pitfall a query exercises - range comparisons and null - than by surface measures such as document count or the number of composed rules. Prepending a verified rule sheet helps unevenly; executing the original filter against the engine yields reliable match sets, but delegation must be checked: on 28% of items (averaged over three runs) one model's executed filters never passed a canonical check against the intended query, and it answered about 22 of them wrong, while the other three passed on every item. We release the benchmark, the mongod oracle, and the evaluation code with all prompts at https://github.com/research-repo-bai/MongoBench.

items.title: When Routine Operations Break Architectural Pattern Relationships in LLM Agent Harnesses
items.author: Boming Xia, Qinghua Lu, Dino Sejdinovic, Liming Zhu
items.content: LLM agent harnesses distribute tool mediation, state management and safety guardrails across native services, independently written plugins and configuration. Routine operations can change the runtime order or retained state that architectural pattern relationships require, without any code change. We study five relationships associated with the Guardrail Enforcement Point, Autonomy Controller and Blackboard patterns across five released harnesses, analysing a main sample of fourteen independently written plugins. Using PatternOps, our assessment procedure, we trace requirements from pattern descriptions, provider documentation and deployment profiles to the providers that realise them and the records that decide them. We then compare alternative allocations under supported operations. Such operations broke relationships silently: after a plugin was reapplied or an allow rule saved, policy stopped evaluating edits while every plugin stayed active, and a prohibited edit executed. Which alternatives qualified depended on the requirement. Allocations that kept the required order, or kept or rebuilt the needed state, held on their tested paths and operation sequences, while others prevented prohibited effects but missed edits rejected elsewhere.
